title: IELTS Speaking forecast Sep–Dec 2026: topics and how to answer
h1: IELTS Speaking forecast September–December 2026: topic families and how to build your answer
description: The IELTS Speaking topic families Vietnamese prep sites predict for September–December 2026, and how to build your own answer instead of memorising one.
text: Skip to main content Jurassic English ™ Kids Academy (5–12) Ages 9–18 IELTS Writing New AI Speaking Mocks Pricing Products & prices English EN Tiếng Việt Tiếng Việt Book Baseline · 690k₫ Baseline · 690k₫ Learning resources IELTS Speaking forecast September–December 2026: topic families and how to build your answer Mr. Jay Adams (CELTA) · 14 October 2026 Topic families compiled on 14 October 2026 from public forecasts on several Vietnamese test-prep sites. Jurassic English™ is independent and not affiliated with British Council, IDP or Cambridge University Press & Assessment. This is a teacher's advice, not official IELTS guidance. English Tiếng Việt Learning resources Key facts IELTS does not publish its Speaking questions. Every "forecast" is an unofficial guess by prep sites, based on what candidates report after their test. In Vietnam, September to December is usually labelled "quý 3" (prep sites split the year into three forecast periods: January–April, May–August, September–December). This guide lists topic families only: no copied question lists, no sample answers. The real questions may differ. What works on any question is a sequence of thinking: answer, reason, example, extend. A Jurassic AI Speaking score is a practice estimate, not an official IELTS score. Close to test day, many learners download a fifty-topic forecast with a model answer for each, and try to memorise as much as they can. Then the examiner asks the question from a slightly different angle, and the prepared answer no longer fits. A forecast is still useful. It tells you what kinds of topics are being reported, so a question about mirrors or keys does not catch you off guard. It does not tell you how to take an idea somewhere. This guide covers both. What a forecast is, and what it is not It is a topic list compiled by prep sites, mostly from what candidates remember after the test. It is not: The test. IELTS does not publish Speaking questions in advance and does not endorse any forecast. A promise. Some sites advertise very high hit rates. Read those numbers as marketing. A list of answers to memorise. The public band descriptors on ielts.org mention memorised language at the lower bands, as something different from real language ability. The same everywhere. Each site's list differs, and some say they are still updating. Use a forecast to choose what to practise , then practise how to build an answer . When the real question differs, the skill still works. Part 1 topic families, September–December 2026 Part 1 lasts about 4–5 minutes of short questions about you and daily life. The forecasts we read list roughly thirty to fifty Part 1 topics, which group into about ten families. Each appeared in most of the sources we read. You and where you live: work or studies, home, hometown, your area or city. Daily rhythm: mornings, evenings, tiredness, tidiness, days off. Small everyday objects: mirrors, keys, shoes, watches, sunglasses, headphones, clothes. Technology and the internet: social media, websites, computers and tablets, typing. Entertainment and the arts: music, singing, art, films, jokes, sports programmes. History, buildings and science: history, old buildings, science, space and stars. Outdoors and getting around: parks, cars, walking, travelling, sport. People and manners: teachers, names, politeness, friends. Shopping and advertising. Dreams: the ones you have asleep, and the ones you have for the future. Part 2 and Part 3 topic families, September–December 2026 Part 2 gives you a cue card, one minute to prepare and one to two minutes to talk. Part 3 is a discussion that takes the Part 2 topic into broader questions. Describe a person: someone who solved a problem cleverly, a childhood friend, someone who runs a successful business, someone who grows plants, someone good at languages, an older person you admire. Describe a place or building: a tall building, a river or lake, a home you would visit but not live in, a place you recommend, a quiet, noisy or crowded place. Technology and media: a power cut or device problem, an app, a time you could not use your phone, a social media video, local news, a film, an advert with a famous person. Decisions, plans and change: an important decision, a changed plan, a changed opinion, a recent change, a long-term goal. Food and gifts: a special cake, food for a special occasion, a gift. Learning and languages: how you learn a language, learning without a teacher, a course. Environment and rules: a new law you would introduce, an environmental law, a natural place. An experience or event: a traffic jam, a very early start, group work, an unanswered message, an event you organised, a low-cost day out. Money and treasured objects: saving money, overspending, a family heirloom. Part 3 (our inference, not a source list): Part 3 is usually the abstract version of the Part 2 family. "A person who solved a problem" leads to problem-solving at school or work; "a new law" leads to the roles of government and citizens. How to build an answer: answer, reason, example, extend This is not a sentence frame. It is four questions you ask yourself before you speak; the content must be yours. Answer: say your main point in the first sentence. Reason: one real reason, more specific than "it's convenient". Example: one real moment, person or place from your life. Extend: a consequence, a comparison (then and now, you and others), or a condition. Family 1 (Part 1): small everyday objects. Asked about keys, mirrors or watches: do I use it much (answer)? Why, and what habit is it tied to (reason)? When did I last use, forget or lose it (example; illustrative: "…last week I locked myself out")? How has it changed over time (extend)? The real detail is what makes a Part 1 answer come alive. Family 2 (Part 2): a person who solved a problem cleverly. In the minute of preparation, write four keywords, not sentences: who the person is; what the problem was and why it was hard; what they did, step by step (illustrative: "…instead of calling a repair shop, she…"), the longest part; what you learned. If the story is real, you remember the order, not the words. Family 3 (Part 3): environment and rules. Asked whether government or individuals should protect the environment: take a clear position (answer); give a general reason (reason); point to something you have seen in your city or country (example; illustrative: "…plastic-bag rules in some supermarkets"); add a downside, a condition or a prediction (extend). An ielts.org article on band 6 and band 7 makes the same point: stronger speakers build arguments, not just opinions. A four-week plan Week 1: three hard Part 1 families, five questions a day, recorded. Week 2: three Part 2 families, one cue card a day, four keywords, two minutes. Week 3: two Part 3 questions for each of those cards; practise "extend". Week 4: mix everything, including topics not on any forecast. Each week, count two things in your recordings: mid-sentence hesitations and real ideas per answer. FAQ Which months does the quý 3/2026 forecast cover? Vietnamese prep sites use "quý 3/2026" for September to December 2026. The label is theirs, not IELTS's. Is an IELTS Speaking forecast the real test? No. IELTS does not publish Speaking questions. Forecasts are unofficial guesses. Should I memorise the sample answers in a forecast? No. Practise the sequence: answer, reason, example, extend. Does Part 1 change much between periods? Families such as work or studies, home and hometown appear in most forecasts. Secure those first. Is a Jurassic AI Speaking score an IELTS score? No. It is an AI practice estimate with an uncertainty range, not an official IELTS score. Typed answers cannot be assessed for pronunciation. Is Jurassic English linked to British Council, IDP or Cambridge? No. Jurassic English™ is independent, and this advice is unofficial. Practise forecast topics, then measure where you are Jurassic AI Speaking (adults 18+): a full three-part mock, typed or spoken (speaking mode is a limited beta), with a report that quotes your own answers and names one priority. Practice estimate, not an official IELTS score. From 79.000₫ per test. https://jurassicenglish.com/ai-speaking/vi Live Speaking Baseline: about 15–20 minutes speaking with a Jurassic English assessor, ending with your primary constraint and next step. 690.000₫. https://jurassicenglish.com/ai-speaking/vi/baseline Jurassic AI Speaking is for adults 18 and over. If you are under 18, show this page to a parent. title: Online IELTS Speaking Coaching for Adults: A Buyer Guide | Jurassic English™
h1: Online IELTS Speaking Coaching for Adults: A Buyer Guide
description: An adult buyer guide to online IELTS Speaking coaching: free practice, paid live baseline, one-to-one lessons, assessment limits and booking checks.
text: Skip to main content Jurassic English ™ Kids Academy (5–12) Ages 9–18 IELTS Writing New AI Speaking Mocks Pricing Products & prices Book Baseline · 690k₫ Baseline · 690k₫ Adult IELTS Speaking Online IELTS Speaking Coaching for Adults: A Buyer Guide For adult learners in Vietnam: start with free independent practice, consider a paid live baseline, then decide whether one-to-one coaching fits. Overseas learners should confirm payment and timezone compatibility before booking. Learning resources / Adult IELTS Speaking Published 2026-10-14 · Jurassic English™ editorial team Who this guide is for This English-language guide is for adults aged 18+ considering online IELTS Speaking coaching, initially in Vietnam. It is not the young-learner programme or a parent enquiry page. Adults overseas can use the practice guidance, but should confirm adult session eligibility, payment support and timezone compatibility in the booking flow before paying. 1. Start with free independent practice Use a small task to see whether you can apply a useful change yourself. The One Change challenge uses an illustrative written answer: choose an improvement, explore why it helps, then try a fresh topic in your own words. Speak your attempt aloud and note one question you would like a coach to review. Try the free One Change practice challenge . This is independent practice, not a free personalised speaking assessment or an IELTS band score. You do not need to buy a session to use the challenge. 2. Consider a paid live speaking baseline If you need feedback on how you actually speak, review the paid live baseline as a possible next step. Bring your exam goal, target date, recent practice difficulties and questions about feedback. Confirm adult suitability and what is included before booking; this guide does not promise a session length, report or available slot. A live spoken sample can give a coach evidence of delivery, intelligibility, hesitation, wording and how you respond to follow-up questions. It can help identify a practice priority for the performance observed. Ask which speaking tasks and criteria the session covers, and how the coach will explain the evidence behind any practice estimate. Review the paid live Speaking Baseline and booking details . Live speaking and typed practice are different evidence Typed practice can show word choice, grammar and visible organization. It cannot establish pronunciation, spoken pace, hesitation or real-time interaction. A polished written answer is not evidence of equivalent spoken performance. AI feedback may be wrong and should be checked where it matters. The official IELTS Speaking test has three parts: familiar-topic questions, an individual long turn and a wider discussion. The public criteria cover fluency and coherence, lexical resource, grammatical range and accuracy, and pronunciation. These criteria explain why spoken evidence matters; they do not make a coaching session an official test. What one session cannot establish A baseline is a limited practice sample, not an official IELTS result, a complete measure of ability across every topic or a prediction of your exam score. Connection quality, unfamiliar topics and nerves can affect the sample. Any practice band estimate is provisional. One session cannot establish lasting improvement; that requires later independent attempts and review over time. There are no score guarantees, guaranteed band increases or promised exam outcomes. Practice estimates are not an official IELTS score. Jurassic English is independent of British Council, IDP IELTS and Cambridge University Press & Assessment, the joint owners of IELTS, and its preparation does not imply IELTS endorsement. 3. Decide whether one-to-one coaching fits Consider paid 1:1 coaching when you want guided spoken practice and feedback on a specific priority. A useful lesson plan should connect an observed difficulty to a strategy, a guided attempt, a fresh independent attempt and a manageable follow-up. Ask how the coach would compare attempts rather than simply provide a memorized answer. Continuing independently is also a reasonable choice if you can identify and practise your next step. A baseline does not oblige you to buy further lessons. Review one-to-one coaching options and booking details . Before paying: confirm the practical details Adult eligibility and whether the session fits your goal and exam timeline. Current price, currency, accepted payment methods and any applicable fees in the booking flow. Available dates, the displayed timezone and the corresponding local time where you will attend, including daylight-saving changes overseas. Session duration, online meeting platform, technical requirements and the feedback or follow-up included. Cancellation, rescheduling and refund terms, and the coach's relevant experience or credentials if those matter to your decision. If adult eligibility, payment or scheduling is unclear, seek confirmation through booking before paying. No payment method, qualification, availability, price or result is promised here. description: Accessibility statement for the Jurassic English™ website, outlining standards we follow and how to request accessibility support.
text: Skip to main content Jurassic English ™ Kids Academy (5–12) Ages 9–18 IELTS Writing New AI Speaking Mocks Pricing Products & prices English EN Tiếng Việt Tiếng Việt Free sample pack Free sample pack Back to Jurassic English Legal Accessibility Statement Effective Date : March 2026 · Last Updated : March 21, 2026 OUR COMMITMENT World Wise Learning is committed to ensuring that all Jurassic English™ digital platforms and curriculum materials are accessible to every user, including individuals with disabilities. We actively work to meet internationally recognised accessibility standards. 1 . Our Commitment to Accessibility World Wise Learning believes that access to high-quality education should be equitable and inclusive. We are committed to designing and maintaining digital platforms and curriculum materials that are accessible to the widest possible audience, regardless of ability, disability, or the assistive technologies they use. Our accessibility commitment is aligned with the following frameworks: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1 Level AA — the international standard for digital accessibility; Universal Design for Learning (UDL) — embedded in Our curriculum design to provide multiple means of engagement, representation, and expression; UNESCO Education for All and Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) principles; Applicable national and regional legislation, including the UK Equality Act 2010 and equivalent international provisions. 2 . Conformance Status Our digital platforms are partially conformant with WCAG 2.1 Level AA. "Partially conformant" means that some parts of the content do not yet fully conform to the standard. We are actively working to address known gaps and improve conformance across all platforms and materials. Criterion Detail Target Standard WCAG 2.1 Level AA Conformance Level Partially Conformant Assessment Method Internal review by World Wise Learning accessibility team Assessment Date March 21, 2026 Next Scheduled Review March 2027 3 . Accessible Features Currently Implemented The following accessibility features are in place across Our platforms: Keyboard navigability: Core platform functions can be accessed without a mouse; Screen reader compatibility: Semantic HTML and ARIA labels support assistive technology; Text alternatives: Images include descriptive alt text attributes; Colour contrast: Text and UI elements are designed to meet minimum contrast ratios (4.5:1 for normal text); Resizable text: Content reflows appropriately when text is scaled up to 200% without horizontal scrolling; Captions: Video content includes closed captions where available; Consistent navigation: Navigation menus and page structures are consistent throughout; Error identification: Form errors are clearly identified and described in text; Language identification: All pages include a defined language attribute in the page header. 4 . Known Limitations We acknowledge the following known limitations and are actively working to address them: Some older PDF curriculum documents may not be fully compatible with screen reader technology. These are being progressively updated. Certain third-party embedded tools (e.g., video players and interactive assessments) may not fully conform to WCAG 2.1 AA. We are working with third-party providers to improve conformance. Complex data tables in some assessment materials may require additional navigation support for screen reader users. Audio descriptions for all video content are not yet universally available. This is being addressed in Our content production pipeline. If you encounter an accessibility barrier not listed above, please contact Us as described in Section 7. 5 . Curriculum Accessibility Jurassic English™ curriculum materials are designed using Universal Design for Learning (UDL) principles. For users in the United Kingdom: The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) is responsible for enforcing equality legislation. For matters relating to public sector bodies and accessibility regulations, you may also contact the relevant monitoring body. For private sector services, you may seek independent legal advice. For users in other jurisdictions: Please refer to your applicable national disability rights or equality authority for information on your rights and available remedies. 9 . What Are Cookies? Cookies are small text files placed on your device (computer, tablet, or smartphone) when you visit a website or use a digital platform. Strictly necessary cookies cannot be disabled as they are essential to platform functionality. 5.2 Browser Settings You can manage and delete cookies through your browser settings. Most modern browsers allow you to: View all cookies currently stored on your device; Block cookies from specific or all websites; Delete all cookies at the end of each browsing session. title: Jurassic Thinking Cycle™ Methodology | Jurassic English™
h1: The methodology that separates structured thinking from surface fluency.
description: Explore the four-stage reasoning architecture behind Jurassic English™ lessons: analyze, evaluate, justify, and reflect.
text: Skip to main content Jurassic English ™ Kids Academy (5–12) Ages 9–18 IELTS Writing New AI Speaking Mocks Pricing Products & prices English EN Tiếng Việt Tiếng Việt Free sample pack Free sample pack Illustration Institutional partner for schools and universities: WorldWise Learning (opens in a new tab) Back to main site Instructional Architecture Jurassic Thinking Cycle™ The methodology that separates structured thinking from surface fluency. The Jurassic Thinking Cycle™ is not a teaching style. It is the instructional architecture through which Jurassic English™ moves students from text comprehension to moral evaluation to evidence-based argument — at every level, in every lesson. Request an Audit Sprint Book a Discovery Call The Problem with Generic ELT Most English programmes produce test results. Very few produce thinkers. The standard ELT model optimises for measurable output: scores, pass rates, level progressions. What it rarely measures — and rarely builds — is the capacity to reason, evaluate evidence, and argue from a position. That is the gap Jurassic English™ was designed to close. Test-Prep Mimicry Students learn to replicate answer formats without developing the reasoning behind them. Fluency becomes performative. The gap between language ability and thinking ability widens with every level. Teacher-Dependent Delivery When methodology lives inside individual teachers rather than a shared curriculum framework, quality becomes a function of who is in the room. Programmes cannot scale what they cannot codify. Comprehension Without Critique Reading programmes that stop at literal recall produce students who can decode text but cannot interrogate it. Critical thinking is not a bonus stage added at higher levels. It is the point of the lesson — at every level. The Jurassic Thinking Cycle™ Four stages. One architecture. Every lesson. The Thinking Cycle is the instructional sequence that structures every Jurassic English™ lesson. It is not an overlay applied to content — it is the architecture through which content is taught. The sequence is not optional. Each stage builds on the last. Stage 01 Analyze What is the text doing, and how is it doing it? Students encounter the text as a structured object. They identify what is being said, how it is constructed, and what choices the author has made. This is not comprehension — it is the first act of critical engagement. The text becomes something to interrogate, not simply decode. See the Analyze stage in full Stage 02 Evaluate Is the argument sound, and what does the evidence actually support? Students assess the quality, validity, and intent of what they have read. They are asked to judge — not just describe. Is the argument sound? Is the evidence sufficient? Does the author's perspective contain assumptions? This stage builds the habit of calibrated scepticism. See the Evaluate stage in full Stage 03 Justify What is my position, and how do I defend it with evidence? Students construct and defend a position using evidence from the text. They learn that argument is not opinion — it is a claim supported by reasoning and evidence. The writing produced at this stage is academically structured, not spontaneous expression. See the Justify stage in full Stage 04 Reflect What does this text reveal about a question that matters beyond the page? Students consider what the text, the discussion, and their own argument reveal about a broader question — ethical, social, ecological. This is the stage at which English becomes a vehicle for moral reasoning, not just linguistic performance. See the Reflect stage in full Authentic Literature The text is not the vehicle. The text is the methodology. Jurassic English™ uses authentic literature — real books, not controlled readers — because the complexity that drives reasoning cannot be manufactured. Simplified texts produce simplified thinking. Complexity That Earns Its Place Authentic texts contain the authorial choices — structure, perspective, tension, ambiguity — that make the Analyze and Evaluate stages meaningful. There is nothing to evaluate in a text written to be easy. The difficulty is the point. Moral and Ethical Material Literature from diverse traditions and ecological contexts provides the material that makes the Reflect stage academically serious rather than decorative. The texts are selected for the questions they raise, not only for the language they contain. CEFR Progression Through Reasoning Demand Progression in Jurassic English™ is tracked through text complexity and reasoning demand — not simply vocabulary load or grammar scope. A student's CEFR level is a description of what they can think through, not only what they can say. Regulation Before Reasoning The cognitive layer that most curricula skip entirely. The Jurassic Thinking Cycle™ operates on a principle that is rarely foregrounded in ELT: students cannot reason effectively if they are dysregulated. Emotional and cognitive regulation is not a welfare consideration — it is an instructional prerequisite. Dysregulation Blocks Reasoning A student who is anxious about being wrong cannot evaluate an argument — their cognitive resource is allocated to self-protection, not reasoning. Treating this as a discipline or motivation failure is both inaccurate and counterproductive. Ambiguity Tolerance Is Teachable A student who has not learned to tolerate ambiguity will resolve a complex text by choosing the simplest interpretation. That is not a reading failure. It is a regulatory one. The Thinking Cycle builds ambiguity tolerance systematically, not incidentally. Teachers Are Prepared, Not Just Informed Jurassic English™ teachers are prepared in co-regulation techniques and the distinction between a reasoning failure and a regulatory one — so that their intervention is accurate, targeted, and does not inadvertently penalise a student for a cognitive state rather than a cognitive gap. Methodology Fidelity A methodology is only as strong as the governance that protects it. The Jurassic Thinking Cycle™ is a precise instructional architecture. When it is applied inconsistently — adapted freely by individual teachers, compressed for time, or layered on top of an existing programme without structural change — it stops working as designed. 01 Sequence Integrity The four stages are sequential, not optional. Skipping Evaluate to reach Justify faster produces argument without calibration. Compressing Analyze into comprehension produces students who defend positions they have not properly examined. The sequence is the methodology. 02 Teacher Preparation Teachers require explicit preparation in the Thinking Cycle before delivering it to students. A teacher who has not been trained to facilitate Evaluate cannot model it — and cannot distinguish a student who is struggling with the text from a student who is struggling with the cognitive demand of the stage. 03 Institutional Architecture Methodology fidelity requires that the curriculum framework — not individual teacher preference — governs what happens in the classroom. This is what the WorldWise Learning institutional model provides: a shared architecture that survives staff turnover, scales across centres, and can be audited. The Next Step If the methodology is right, the entry point is straightforward. Jurassic English™ and WorldWise Learning offer structured institutional entry points — designed to move from first contact to pilot in a defined sequence. The Discovery Call is where your specific institutional context is assessed against the framework in detail. Request an Audit Sprint Book a Discovery Call · Explore the Curriculum Series This page is a public summary of the methodology architecture. Full programme documentation, teacher preparation materials, and institutional governance frameworks are provided through the WorldWise Learning engagement pathway. title: Jurassic English™ Pilot Programme — 6-8 Week Institutional Evaluation
h1: A governed pilot framework for institutional adoption decisions.
description: A structured 6-8 week Jurassic English™ pilot pathway for schools, academies, and training centres. Measure student reasoning evidence, teacher fidelity, progression fit, and implementation readiness before wider rollout.
text: Skip to main content Jurassic English ™ Kids Academy (5–12) Ages 9–18 IELTS Writing New AI Speaking Mocks Pricing Products & prices English EN Tiếng Việt Tiếng Việt Free sample pack Free sample pack Back to main site Institutional Pilot Programme 6–8 Week Evaluation Pathway A governed pilot framework for institutional adoption decisions. The Jurassic English Pilot Programme gives schools, academies, and training centres a structured way to evaluate academic fit, teacher readiness, operational load, and commercial rollout logic before committing to full licensing or multi-class deployment. Request Full Pilot Pack Request a Pilot Consultation Book a Discovery Call Watch the 60-second founder vision film ( Made with Google Vids: AI video and AI voice . Scenes are illustrative, not real lessons or clients. ) Adoption pathway Evidence before scale commitment Step 1 Audit Sprint Step 2 Pilot Programme Step 3 Executive Review Step 4 Licensing / Scale What the Pilot Is A structured institutional evaluation framework, not a sample lesson. The pilot creates a controlled evidence base around a defined learner group, named implementation roles, agreed decision gates, and a final rollout recommendation. It is built for procurement, academic leadership, and investor-grade proof of adoption readiness. A scoped learner cohort, class level, or programme segment agreed before launch. A practical implementation plan aligned to the school or centre context. Teacher orientation and delivery guidance before classroom use begins. Evidence collection across student work, teacher fidelity, progression fit, and operational load. Who It Is For Designed for institutions that need proof before scale. The pilot is most useful when a buyer has moved beyond general interest and needs a structured way to test fit, feasibility, and implementation risk. School Leaders You need board-ready evidence before approving a new curriculum pathway. Use the pilot to evaluate whether Jurassic English supports your standards, academic positioning, teacher capacity, and parent-facing curriculum story. Academic Directors You need to know whether the methodology holds up in live classrooms. Use the pilot to assess teacher readiness, lesson fidelity, progression logic, and the quality of student reasoning evidence. Centre Owners You need a low-risk way to differentiate before investing in full rollout. Use the pilot to test commercial fit, operational load, teacher adoption, and whether the programme creates a defensible market position. Structure Four phases. Four decision gates. One adoption recommendation. The exact scope depends on institution size and readiness, but every pilot follows the same operating logic: prepare the institution, activate classroom delivery, measure implementation evidence, then decide the correct commercial pathway. 0 1 Discovery and Alignment 0 2 MVP Design 0 3 Execution and Data Collection 0 4 Conversion and Scale Preparation 01 Setup Scope and Readiness Review Purpose Define the institutional problem, pilot boundary, and success criteria before any classroom activity begins. Activities Confirm learner group, teacher roles, implementation window, and timetable constraints. Review standards context, materials access, stakeholder expectations, and commercial intent. Outputs Pilot scope note Readiness checklist Success measures Decision Gate Proceed only if the institution can name accountable roles, protect the pilot window, and supply baseline context. 02 Week 1 Teacher and Admin Orientation Purpose Prepare the delivery team to implement the methodology consistently enough for evidence to be meaningful. Activities Orient teachers to the Jurassic Thinking Cycle, selected materials, and classroom routines. Brief administrators on evidence capture, review cadence, and escalation expectations. Outputs Orientation record Delivery protocol Evidence capture plan Decision Gate Proceed only if the teacher team can demonstrate delivery readiness and the sponsor accepts the evidence protocol. 03 Weeks 2-7 Guided Classroom Implementation Purpose Run the pilot in live classrooms while measuring academic value, teacher fidelity, and operational feasibility. Activities Deliver agreed pilot lessons with structured check-ins and review touchpoints. Collect student work, teacher feedback, observation notes, and implementation friction signals. Outputs Evidence log Teacher fidelity notes Operational risk register Decision Gate Continue, narrow, or pause if evidence quality, teacher capacity, or operational load falls outside the agreed threshold. 04 Week 8 Pilot Review and Rollout Recommendation Purpose Convert pilot evidence into a clear institutional decision and commercially realistic next step. Activities Review academic evidence, operational findings, stakeholder feedback, and commercial readiness. Hold a final debrief with the sponsor, academic lead, and implementation lead. Outputs Pilot summary KPI block Rollout recommendation Decision Gate Select the next pathway: advisory continuation, institutional MVP, scale readiness, revised pilot, or no rollout. Governance Layer Every pilot has named accountability. The pilot is managed as an institutional workstream, not as a casual classroom experiment. Roles, cadence, and escalation logic are agreed before launch so evidence can be trusted by leadership teams. Operating model Named owners, weekly evidence review, sponsor escalation. Pilot Sponsor Academic Lead Implementation Lead Teacher Champion Review cadence Weekly pilot review during active implementation, with a setup checkpoint and final debrief. Escalation logic Academic, operational, or stakeholder risks are escalated to the Sponsor when they threaten evidence quality, timeline, or decision readiness. Pilot Sponsor Senior institutional owner who protects the pilot mandate, confirms commercial intent, and receives the final recommendation. Academic Lead Curriculum or academic decision-maker responsible for standards fit, learner placement, and interpretation of evidence. Implementation Lead Operational owner who coordinates timetable, materials access, communications, and pilot administration. Teacher Champion Classroom practitioner who models adoption, surfaces delivery friction, and supports teacher feedback quality. Review cadence Weekly pilot review during active implementation, with a setup checkpoint and final debrief. Escalation logic Academic, operational, or stakeholder risks are escalated to the Sponsor when they threaten evidence quality, timeline, or decision readiness. What Gets Measured The pilot is judged by evidence, not enthusiasm. Each pilot produces a practical evidence base that helps institutional buyers decide whether Jurassic English should move into a larger implementation pathway. 0 1 Teacher outcomes Fidelity and readiness Delivery confidence, routine consistency, planning load, and support needs. 0 2 Student outcomes Reasoning evidence Comprehension quality, evidence use, discussion, justification, and written response. 0 3 Parent outcomes Confidence signals Clarity of learning value, visible progress artefacts, and communication readiness. 0 4 Institutional/system outcomes Rollout feasibility Timetable fit, staffing demand, admin load, licensing readiness, and scale logic. Student Reasoning Evidence Quality of comprehension, evidence use, justification, discussion, and written response across selected lesson moments. Teacher Fidelity How consistently teachers can apply the Thinking Cycle, questioning routines, discussion protocols, and feedback expectations. Progression Fit Whether the selected level, language demand, text complexity, and assessment expectations match the institution's learners. Operational Load Scheduling, preparation time, administrator oversight, parent communication needs, and training implications. Commercial Readiness Whether the programme can support a credible full rollout, licensing pathway, or staged partnership conversation. Support Included Teachers and administrators are not left to interpret the programme alone. The pilot includes enough support to make the evidence meaningful while keeping the commitment contained. Pilot scope confirmation and implementation checklist. Teacher orientation for the selected pilot pathway. Administrator briefing on measures, timeline, and evidence expectations. Review touchpoints during implementation. Student work and teacher feedback review. Final pilot summary with rollout recommendation. Commercial Model Three pilot pathways for different levels of readiness. The commercial model keeps adoption low-risk while preserving seriousness. Each pathway is scoped before launch and designed to produce an evidence-backed decision, not an open-ended trial. Advisory-First Pilot Path 1 Fit Best for institutions still clarifying curriculum problem, standards pressure, or internal readiness. Model Consultative pilot design, materials review, leadership advisory, and limited implementation planning before classroom activation. Decision use Use this pathway to decide whether the institution should continue advisory work, launch an MVP, or prepare for scaled licensing. Institutional MVP Pilot Path 2 Fit Best for schools or centres ready to test one learner group, one level, or one defined programme segment. Model A contained classroom pilot with teacher orientation, evidence capture, review cadence, and final rollout recommendation. Decision use Use this pathway to decide whether the institution should continue advisory work, launch an MVP, or prepare for scaled licensing. Scale Readiness Pilot Path 3 Fit Best for multi-class, multi-campus, or school-group buyers evaluating a wider adoption pathway. Model Pilot architecture focused on governance, teacher consistency, operational load, and hub-and-spoke expansion planning. Decision use Use this pathway to decide whether the institution should continue advisory work, launch an MVP, or prepare for scaled licensing. What Institutions Receive Concrete outputs for academic, operational, and commercial review. The pilot produces decision assets that can be reviewed by school leadership, academic directors, owners, and investment stakeholders. Pilot scope and readiness note Teacher orientation and delivery protocol Evidence capture framework Weekly review notes and risk register Student reasoning evidence sample review Teacher fidelity and implementation observations Operational load assessment Final pilot report with rollout recommendation Institutional Proof Assets The pilot sits inside a broader evaluation pack. Jurassic English evaluation materials are structured around three institutional proof assets. They can be requested through the enquiry pathway as part of a serious review conversation. Curriculum Overview Programme architecture, levels, methodology, standards alignment, and institutional use cases. Audit Sprint Overview How the 10-business-day review works, what it examines, and what documents the institution receives. Pilot Programme Overview Pilot scope, measurement model, support rhythm, evidence review, and rollout recommendation format. Reporting Architecture Results are reported in a format leadership teams can use. The reporting model is designed for institutional decision-making now and for future case-study publication once live evidence is approved for external use. Report layer 0 1 Executive Summary Institution context, learner group, pilot duration, implementation scope, evidence quality, and headline recommendation. Report layer 0 2 KPI Block Student reasoning evidence, teacher fidelity indicators, progression fit, operational load, stakeholder confidence, and commercial readiness. Report layer 0 3 Implementation Observations What helped or hindered delivery: timetable fit, materials access, teacher confidence, administrator load, and stakeholder communication. Report layer 0 4 Rollout Recommendation A practical decision: proceed to rollout, extend the pilot, prepare teachers first, adjust level placement, or stop. Investor Logic Why a pilot-first model is commercially defensible. For investors and strategic partners, the pilot model creates a repeatable adoption mechanism. It reduces buyer risk while producing proof assets that support sales, training, licensing, and expansion. Scale 0 1 Reduced adoption risk Institutions can test fit and feasibility before full rollout, lowering the perceived risk of switching curriculum architecture. Scale 0 2 Proof-led sales collateral Each completed pilot can generate structured evidence, case-study inputs, objection handling, and implementation benchmarks. Scale 0 3 Lower-friction conversion The pilot bridges the gap between interest and procurement by creating a defined next step with bounded scope and clear decision logic. Scale 0 4 Hub-and-spoke expansion logic A successful pilot can expand from one class to a year group, campus, school group, teacher-training cohort, or regional partner network. Next Step Request a pilot consultation. Use the enquiry pathway if your institution is ready to evaluate Jurassic English in a defined, evidence-producing pilot. If you are still exploring fit, begin with a Discovery Call. Request Full Pilot Pack Request a Pilot Consultation Book a Discovery Call For centres: Pilot Class Launch Kit Pilot scope is confirmed before any implementation begins. The WorldWise Learning team will recommend a smaller entry point if your institution is not yet ready for a pilot. title: Level 1: Foundation Syllabus — Ages 4–8 years | Jurassic English™
h1: Level 1: Foundation
description: The full Jurassic English™ Level 1: Foundation curriculum syllabus for ages 4–8 years. Core texts, term breakdown, assessment methods, eco-reasoning strand, and CEFR progression (Pre-A1 → A1).
text: Skip to main content Jurassic English ™ Kids Academy (5–12) Ages 9–18 IELTS Writing New AI Speaking Mocks Pricing Products & prices English EN Tiếng Việt Tiếng Việt Free sample pack Free sample pack Back Curriculum Syllabus · Academic Year 2025–26 Level 1: Foundation First Stories. First Thinking. Welcome to Level 1: Foundation — the beginning of an extraordinary thinking journey. At this level, your child will explore the world through beautifully crafted picture books and short stories. But these are not ordinary story-times. Every book in the Jurassic English™ programme has been chosen because it raises a real question — about fairness, feelings, community, or our place in the natural world. From the very first lesson, your child will be asked to think out loud, share their views, and use the words of the text to explain what they believe. By the end of this year, your child will not merely read stories. They will analyse them, evaluate characters' choices, and write their first justified opinions. View Level Details Level at a Glance Everything you need to know at a glance Age Range 6–8 years CEFR Range Pre-A1 → A1 Total Lessons 40 structured lessons per academic year Lesson Duration 40–60 minutes per lesson CEFR Progression Pre-A1 → A1 (approx. 90–100 instructional hours) Cognitive Focus BICS — phonics, high-frequency vocabulary, context-embedded language Text Complexity Picture books and predictable narratives Eco-Reasoning Strand Local nature, seasons, and animal relationships Core Texts Literature selected to develop real thinking Every text is chosen because it raises questions that do not have easy answers. 10 core texts per year; 4 structured lessons per text. There's an Alligator Under My Bed Mayer Imagination, courage, and problem-solving The Name Jar Choi Identity, naming, and cultural belonging A Chair for My Mother Williams Family resilience, community, and generosity Owl Moon Eco Yolen Wonder in the natural world; patience and presence Additional texts: 6 additional titles are selected per WWL text criteria in consultation with the school community. All selected texts meet the five-criterion standard for diverse cultural perspectives and ecological richness. Academic Year Term-by-term curriculum map 1 Term 1 Lessons 1–13 · Units 1–3 Introduce the Jurassic Thinking Cycle™ Guided Analyze — 'What do we notice?' with partner share and sentence frames First oral Evaluate: 'Was this a good or bad choice?' Eco warm-up: 2-minute outdoor observation before each lesson 2 Term 2 Lessons 14–27 · Units 4–7 First written justification sentences (Claim + Evidence) Introduce personal Reflect prompt: 'This connects to my life because…' Eco strand active: informal nature journaling begins Ecological prompt: 'What do we name things in nature? Why does naming matter?' 3 Term 3 Lessons 28–40 · Units 8–10 Full Thinking Cycle across all four stages with light scaffolding Portfolio introduction: students choose their best justification sentence CEFR self-assessment on Pre-A1 / A1 descriptor grid Reading celebration — students share their reasoning journey Assessment Assessment tracks the quality of reasoning. All written justification tasks are assessed using the WWL Four-Level Reasoning Rubric. Lesson Observation Every lesson Teacher notes who provides evidence vs. opinion-only responses. Prompts and redirects with clarification questions. Written Justification 2–3 per week One-sentence Claim + Evidence response. Feedback returned within 24 hours. Sentence frames available. Exit Ticket End of each lesson One Reflect prompt; one sentence. Teacher sorts into Ready / Nearly / Not Yet to plan next lesson. Portfolio Per unit × 10 Student selects their best justification sentence and annotates: 'This shows my best thinking because…' CEFR Self-Assessment Each term Student marks current level on Pre-A1 / A1 descriptor grid. Teacher confirms or challenges in conference. Year-End Growth Narrative End of year 'My reasoning journey this year…' — teacher reads holistically to inform Level 2 placement. WWL Four-Level Reasoning Rubric The standard applied to all written work 1 Emerging States a position without support. Opinion only — no warrant. No textual evidence cited. 2 Developing Cites evidence without clear connection. Evidence present; warrant absent or unclear. 3 Proficient Links evidence to claim with clear reasoning. Claim + Evidence + Warrant all present. Evidence selected purposefully. 4 Advanced Anticipates counterarguments; extends to broader implications. Full CEIW with multiple evidence points. Eco-Learning Thread Local nature, seasons, and animal relationships At Foundation level, eco-learning begins with wonder. Books such as Owl Moon invite children to slow down, notice the living world, and feel a sense of connection and responsibility. Children begin an informal nature journal — drawing and labelling what they observe. The Ecological Reflection prompt at this level asks: 'What do we name things in nature? Why does naming matter?' Supporting Learning at Home Read aloud together for 15 minutes daily — your voice models fluent, expressive English and builds listening comprehension. After reading, ask: 'Why did the character do that?' — not just 'What happened?' This develops reasoning rather than recall. Take a 5-minute 'observation walk' outside. Ask your child to name 3 living things and describe one relationship between them. Display your child's best justification sentence visibly — visible pride reinforces the reasoning habit. Let your child 'teach you' what they discussed in today's lesson. Explaining to others deepens understanding significantly. Programme Progression Where this level fits Coming from Programme entry point Leading to Level 2: Development Readiness for the next stage Students are ready for Level 2 when they can sustain a focused discussion using textual evidence, write one independent Claim + Evidence sentence, and make a personal connection in their Reflect response. CEFR readiness for A1 is confirmed through end-of-year portfolio review and teacher assessment. Placement is never based on a single test. description: Jurassic English™ Level 2 builds structured reasoning for ages 8–10 through early chapter books, evidence-based writing, and Socratic discussion. Supports A1 to A2 CEFR progression.

h1: Level 2: Development
description: The full Jurassic English™ Level 2: Development curriculum syllabus for ages 8–10 years. Core texts, term breakdown, assessment methods, eco-reasoning strand, and CEFR progression (A1 → A2).
text: Skip to main content Jurassic English ™ Kids Academy (5–12) Ages 9–18 IELTS Writing New AI Speaking Mocks Pricing Products & prices English EN Tiếng Việt Tiếng Việt Free sample pack Free sample pack Back Curriculum Syllabus · Academic Year 2025–26 Level 2: Development Growing Thinkers. Growing Readers. Welcome to Level 2: Development — where thinking becomes a disciplined habit. In this level, your child will move from picture books into chapter books: longer, richer, and full of the moral questions that do not have easy answers. Is it ever right to stay silent when someone is being treated unjustly? What responsibility do we have to animals and to the environment? Your child will learn to use textual evidence to back up their opinions, structure their reasoning in writing, and listen carefully to the arguments of their classmates. By the end of this year, your child will write full justification paragraphs, lead a structured class discussion, and make connections between literature, their own lives, and the living world. View Level Details Level at a Glance Everything you need to know at a glance Age Range 8–10 years CEFR Range A1 → A2 Total Lessons 40 structured lessons per academic year Lesson Duration 40–60 minutes per lesson CEFR Progression A1 → A2 (approx. 180–200 instructional hours) Cognitive Focus Context-Embedded Learning — students describe their world and begin to evaluate it Text Complexity Early chapter books with clear moral dilemmas Eco-Reasoning Strand Environmental consequence, habitat, and food chains Core Texts Literature selected to develop real thinking Every text is chosen because it raises questions that do not have easy answers. 10 core texts per year; 4 structured lessons per text. Charlotte's Web Eco White Friendship, life cycles, and what we owe to other creatures The Hundred Dresses Estes Bullying, moral courage, and the cost of silence Esperanza Rising Ryan Migration, identity, dignity, and resilience The Lorax Eco Seuss Environmental consequence, corporate greed, and ecological stewardship Additional texts: 6 additional titles are selected per WWL text criteria in consultation with the school community. All selected texts meet the five-criterion standard. Academic Year Term-by-term curriculum map 1 Term 1 Lessons 1–13 · Units 1–3 Consolidate Analyze with longer texts — guided annotation, stand-and-point to evidence Evaluate introduced formally: partner discussions with criteria ('Was this fair? By what standard?') Eco strand: Charlotte's Web — food chains, animal intelligence, and what we owe to non-human lives Accountable talk protocols established for whole-group discussion 2 Term 2 Lessons 14–27 · Units 4–7 Full Justify stage: Claim + Evidence + Warrant paragraphs Socratic discussion protocols established The Lorax eco-reasoning unit: 'What responsibility do businesses have to the environment?' Stewardship Challenge introduced: 'What would a responsible member of this ecosystem do?' 3 Term 3 Lessons 28–40 · Units 8–10 Complete Thinking Cycle independently across all four stages Reflect stage: ethical prompt ('Why does this matter for how we live?') Portfolio assembly: students curate their 10 best justification paragraphs CEFR A2 self-assessment and readiness review Assessment Assessment tracks the quality of reasoning. All written justification tasks are assessed using the WWL Four-Level Reasoning Rubric. Lesson Observation Every lesson Teacher notes who distinguishes explicit from implicit information. Prompts with clarification questions. Partner Discussion Every lesson Teacher listens for evaluation criteria. Strong evaluations marked publicly: 'That was an evaluation — you used a criterion.' Written Justification 2–3 per week Claim + Evidence + Warrant paragraph. Feedback within 24 hours. Sentence frame available for Emerging writers. Exit Ticket End of each lesson One Reflect prompt: personal or ecological. Teacher sorts into Ready / Nearly / Not Yet. Portfolio Per unit × 10 Best justification paragraph per unit. Student annotates why this represents their best reasoning. CEFR Self-Assessment Each term Student marks A1 / A2 descriptor grid. Teacher confirms in conference; result informs Term 2 differentiation. WWL Four-Level Reasoning Rubric The standard applied to all written work 1 Emerging States a position without support. Opinion only — no warrant. No textual evidence cited. 2 Developing Cites evidence without clear connection. Evidence present; warrant absent or unclear. 3 Proficient Links evidence to claim with clear reasoning. Claim + Evidence + Warrant all present. Evidence selected purposefully. 4 Advanced Anticipates counterarguments; extends to broader implications. Full CEIW with multiple evidence points. Eco-Learning Thread Environmental consequence, habitat, and food chains Level 2 is where eco-reasoning becomes explicit and structured. Charlotte's Web invites students to ask: 'What do we owe to non-human lives?' The Lorax requires students to evaluate corporate decision-making against ecological consequence. The Stewardship Challenge — 'What would a responsible member of this ecosystem do?' — is introduced as a formal dialogue prompt. Students begin a structured nature observation log. Supporting Learning at Home Encourage your child to read one chapter independently each week and report the most interesting decision a character made — not what happened, but what the character chose. Ask: 'Was that a fair decision?' then follow up: 'What evidence from the story supports your view?' Watch a nature documentary together and discuss: 'Do humans have a responsibility to protect this animal?' Ask your child to read their best justification paragraph aloud, then ask: 'What is the warrant — the connection between your evidence and your claim?' Review your child's CEFR self-assessment each term and celebrate progress on the descriptor grid. Programme Progression Where this level fits Coming from Level 1: Foundation (or programme entry) Leading to Level 3: Expansion Readiness for the next stage Students are ready for Level 3 when they can construct a complete Claim + Evidence + Warrant justification paragraph independently, sustain a 5-minute Socratic discussion using textual evidence, and write a personal reflection that extends beyond summary to evaluation or ethical connection. title: Level 3: Expansion — Ages 10–12 years | Jurassic English™
h1: Level 3: Expansion
description: Jurassic English™ Level 3 develops the Literacy Pivot for ages 10–12, using complex chapter books to build academic reasoning and CEIW writing. Supports A2 to B1 CEFR progression.
text: Skip to main content Jurassic English ™ Kids Academy (5–12) Ages 9–18 IELTS Writing New AI Speaking Mocks Pricing Products & prices English EN Tiếng Việt Tiếng Việt Free sample pack Free sample pack Back to homepage Series Level Detail Level 3: Expansion Complex Texts. Deeper Thinking. Welcome to Level 3: Expansion — the year literature becomes a lens on the world. Researchers call the transition from A2 to B1 the 'Literacy Pivot': the point at which English shifts from describing the immediate world to reasoning about abstract ideas. At this level, students are expected to hold competing interpretations in mind simultaneously and explain how they weigh them. Foundation Development Expansion Mastery Advanced Demo Material View Syllabus Compare All Levels At A Glance Core level profile Age Band 10–12 years CEFR Range A2 → B1 Lessons / Year 40 structured lessons per academic year Core Texts 10 core texts (4 lessons each) Cognitive Focus The Literacy Pivot (Cummins): English transitions from social communication to the medium of academic reasoning across subjects A2 → B1 (approx. 350–400 instructional hours — the Literacy Pivot) Text Complexity Chapter books with ambiguous endings This is the reading focus named in the syllabus for Level 3: Expansion. Competency Focus Four competencies define the work at this level. Critical Thinking Students deconstruct narratives at multiple levels — plot, character motivation, authorial craft, and cultural assumptions. They hold competing interpretations simultaneously. Moral Reasoning Students engage ethical dilemmas that have no single correct answer, using moral philosophy frameworks to construct and defend positions. Structured Reflection Students move between personal, universal, ethical, metacognitive, and ecological reflection — choosing the most generative lens for each text. Academic Expression Students write full CEIW (Claim–Evidence–Warrant–Impact) analytical paragraphs and lead structured Socratic seminars. Assessment Snapshot Assessment tracks the quality of reasoning. All written justification tasks are assessed using the WWL Four-Level Reasoning Rubric. Lesson observation every lesson: teacher notes who identifies competing interpretations and uses Socratic pressing and revoicing to deepen reasoning. Socratic seminar per unit: evaluated on evidence use, response to peers, evaluation criteria, and ecological extension in eco units. CEIW paragraph 2–3 per week: full Claim–Evidence–Warrant–Impact structure with feedback within 24 hours. CEFR self-assessment each term on the A2 / B1 descriptor grid; the Literacy Pivot (B1) is formally confirmed here. Deeper Thinking. Welcome to Level 3: Expansion — the year literature becomes a lens on the world. Researchers call the transition from A2 to B1 the 'Literacy Pivot': the point at which English shifts from describing the immediate world to reasoning about abstract ideas — justice, memory, collective responsibility, ecological survival. This is one of the most significant transitions in a young person's intellectual development, and it is the work of Level 3. At this level, students are expected to hold competing interpretations in mind simultaneously — to say, with intellectual honesty, 'both of these could be right, and here is how I weigh them.' Welcome to the Literacy Pivot. View Level Details Level at a Glance Everything you need to know at a glance Age Range 10–12 years CEFR Range A2 → B1 Total Lessons 40 structured lessons per academic year Lesson Duration 40–60 minutes per lesson CEFR Progression A2 → B1 (approx. 350–400 instructional hours — the Literacy Pivot) Cognitive Focus The Literacy Pivot (Cummins): English transitions from social communication to the medium of academic reasoning Text Complexity Chapter books with ambiguous endings Eco-Reasoning Strand Extinction, conservation, and human-nature conflict Core Texts Literature selected to develop real thinking Every text is chosen because it raises questions that do not have easy answers. 10 core texts per year; 4 structured lessons per text. The Giver Lowry Memory, freedom, and the cost of a controlled society Number the Stars Lowry Moral courage, duty, and the responsibilities of ordinary people Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry Taylor Racial injustice, dignity, and the politics of land and voice Island of the Blue Dolphins Eco O'Dell Survival, isolation, and the ethics of human-nature relationship Additional texts: 6 additional titles are selected per WWL text criteria in consultation with the school community. At minimum 2 eco-integrated units per year per UNESCO ESD requirement. What do the people owe to the island?' 2 Term 2 Lessons 14–27 · Units 4–7 Structured Socratic seminars with student-led discussion facilitation Systems Thinking eco-reasoning probe: 'If we change this one thing in the story, what else changes?' Place-based outdoor observation integrated as lesson warm-up Written debate: take and defend a position, anticipate counterargument 3 Term 3 Lessons 28–40 · Units 8–10 Extended analytical essay: multi-paragraph, CEIW structure throughout Eco-reflection portfolio entry: 'My ecological thinking grew when…' CEFR B1 self-assessment — the formal Literacy Pivot milestone Growth narrative first draft: 'My reasoning journey so far' Assessment Assessment tracks the quality of reasoning. All written justification tasks are assessed using the WWL Four-Level Reasoning Rubric. Lesson Observation Every lesson Teacher notes who identifies competing interpretations. Socratic pressing and revoicing used to deepen reasoning. Socratic Seminar Per unit Student-led discussion. Evaluated on: evidence use, response to peers, evaluation criteria, and ecological extension in eco units. CEIW Paragraph 2–3 per week Full Claim–Evidence–Warrant–Impact structure. Feedback within 24 hours. Developing writers receive partial paragraph frames. Eco-Reasoning Reflection Per eco unit Written response: 'My ecological thinking grew when I…' Teacher checks for genuine ecological engagement vs. surface-level mention. Portfolio Per unit × 10 Best CEIW paragraph + eco-reasoning reflection per eco-designated unit. Student annotates growth evidence. CEFR Self-Assessment Each term Student marks A2 / B1 descriptor grid. The Literacy Pivot (B1) is formally confirmed here — a significant milestone. WWL Four-Level Reasoning Rubric The standard applied to all written work 1 Emerging States a position without support. Opinion only — no warrant. No textual evidence cited. 2 Developing Cites evidence without clear connection. Evidence present; warrant absent or unclear. 3 Proficient Links evidence to claim with clear reasoning. Claim + Evidence + Warrant all present. Evidence selected purposefully. 4 Advanced Anticipates counterarguments; extends to broader implications. Full CEIW with multiple evidence points. Eco-Learning Thread Extinction, conservation, and human-nature conflict Level 3 introduces the full eco-reasoning framework as a formal programme element. At least two units per year carry eco-integrated lesson plans with an Ecological Anchor Question. Students engage the Jurassic Thinking Cycle™ applied to extinction, conservation, and human-nature conflict. The Systems Thinking Probe — 'If we change this, what else changes?' — models interdependence thinking. Supporting Learning at Home Discuss real-world injustice with your child — Level 3 students are ready to connect literature to news, history, and community events. Ask: 'Could there be another interpretation of that character's choice?' — practise holding two reasonable, opposing ideas simultaneously. Encourage a weekly nature journal: 5 minutes of outdoor observation with 3 written observations and a sketch. Read one of your child's CEIW paragraphs and ask: 'What is the Impact — why does your argument matter beyond this story?' Review the B1 CEFR descriptor with your child and celebrate the Literacy Pivot milestone — it is a genuine academic achievement. Illustration How every lesson works, for confident and shy learners 1 Start calm & curious. A relaxed warm-up and pre-taught story words (Word Fossils), so even shy learners feel safe to share. 2 Explore a real book together. Guided by Professor Rex across four illustrated story worlds, students notice character choices, dilemmas and themes. 3 Look closely, weigh the choices, prove it, connect it. Our 4-step thinking routine (Analyze · Evaluate · Justify · Reflect) turns a quick opinion into a reason backed by the text. 4 Add to your child’s Growth Portfolio. Written Word Fossil vocabulary logs, before-and-after paragraph revisions and written teacher observation notes, shared in a plain-language parent update. Illustration Illustrative Teaching Example From a one-line opinion to a supported explanation “As the storm rose, Maya looked at her last dry flare. Point “I think Maya made the right choice...” 2. Proof “...because she fires her last dry flare to warn the lost fishing crew about the reef...” 3. Open Level 4 University & Exam Bridge Level 5 · Advanced Thinker University & Exam Bridge B2 / C1 Handling counter-arguments and carrying reasoning into IELTS, IB, IGCSE and Cambridge essays and interviews. title: Teacher Quality, iPGCE Standards and Methodology Fidelity | Jurassic English™
h1: The curriculum is only as consistent as the teachers who deliver it.
description: Why teacher quality must be structural, not personality-dependent. iPGCE and PGCE qualification standards, Jurassic Thinking Cycle™ methodology preparation, and the delivery governance architecture that makes classroom consistency possible at scale.
text: Skip to main content Jurassic English ™ Kids Academy (5–12) Ages 9–18 IELTS Writing New AI Speaking Mocks Pricing Products & prices English EN Tiếng Việt Tiếng Việt Free sample pack Free sample pack Back to main site Teacher Quality and Delivery Standards iPGCE · PGCE · Methodology Fidelity The curriculum is only as consistent as the teachers who deliver it. Individual teacher talent is not a scalable quality model. When methodology lives inside people rather than inside a shared framework, programme quality becomes a function of staffing — not architecture. WorldWise Learning builds the structures that make delivery consistent, auditable, and improvable. Book a Discovery Call Request an Audit Sprint The Delivery Quality Problem Most teacher quality problems are architecture problems in disguise. Talented individual teachers are an asset. But when a programme's quality depends on individual talent rather than a shared methodology, you have a staffing problem — not a teaching problem. And staffing problems do not respond to professional development. Personality-Dependent Delivery When lesson quality depends on the specific person teaching it, you cannot scale it, replicate it, or audit it. Two teachers covering the same unit in the same week should produce comparable outcomes. Without a shared methodology framework, they rarely do — and there is no principled way to close the gap. Untrained Methodology Delivery A teacher can read the lesson plan and deliver the activities without engaging the instructional architecture behind them. A teacher who has not been prepared in the Thinking Cycle cannot facilitate Evaluate — they can only ask comprehension questions and describe it as critical thinking. The materials are the same. The outcomes are not. No Observable Practice Standard Without a shared, observable practice standard, academic review becomes subjective. You can observe a lesson and form an impression. You cannot observe a lesson and measure it against a defined expectation without a common framework. Impressionistic review does not produce improvable programmes. Professional Qualification Standards Qualification is the floor, not the ceiling. The iPGCE and PGCE represent internationally recognised benchmarks of teaching professionalism — graduate-level preparation covering pedagogy, subject knowledge, and reflective practice. WorldWise Learning uses these qualifications as the professional foundation standard for all partner teachers. But qualification and methodology preparation are distinct requirements. Required Baseline iPGCE International Postgraduate Certificate in Education The postgraduate teaching qualification for educators working in international and independent school contexts. Delivered through UK-accredited providers, the iPGCE establishes a professional foundation in pedagogy, reflective practice, and subject-appropriate teaching methodology. The required professional baseline for all WorldWise Learning partner teachers. UK Professional Standard PGCE Postgraduate Certificate in Education The primary professional teaching qualification for educators in England and Wales. Graduate-level, combining substantial academic study with assessed school placement practice. PGCE-qualified teachers bring the highest level of professional preparation in subject pedagogy and observable teaching practice standards. Recognised by international accreditation bodies. Critical Distinction Beyond Qualification Methodology Preparation Is a Separate Requirement Qualification certifies professional preparation. It does not certify that a teacher can facilitate the Jurassic Thinking Cycle™. Teachers can hold iPGCE certification and deliver mediocre critical thinking lessons — because the Thinking Cycle is a precise instructional architecture that requires specific preparation, not a general competency that any trained teacher automatically possesses. Methodology Preparation Preparing teachers to deliver the architecture, not just the materials. WorldWise Learning teacher development is preparation-first. Teachers are trained in the specific instructional demands of each stage of the Thinking Cycle before they deliver it to students — what to do, how to facilitate it, what good delivery looks like, and what failure at each stage looks like and how to respond accurately. 01 Facilitating Analyze Teachers learn to guide students toward text interrogation rather than surface comprehension. The distinction is precise: comprehension asks what happened; Analyze asks what the text is doing and how it is constructed. A teacher who conflates the two cannot facilitate the stage — and cannot detect when a student is answering a different question than the one being asked. 02 Facilitating Evaluate The hardest stage to prepare for. Teachers must be able to model calibrated scepticism — not opinion, not preference, but structured assessment of argument quality and evidence sufficiency. A teacher who is not comfortable holding a position under intellectual challenge cannot hold this stage. Preparation includes modelling what a valid evaluation looks like across different text types. 03 Facilitating Justify and Reflect Teachers are prepared to support structured academic argument at Justify — not to generate arguments for students, not to accept unsubstantiated claims, and not to reward fluency over precision. At Reflect, teachers are prepared to hold the distinction between personal response and moral reasoning. Both stages require specific facilitation discipline to produce academically valuable work. 04 Regulation Readiness Teachers are prepared in the distinction between a reasoning failure and a regulatory one. A student who produces a weak Evaluate response may be dysregulated rather than under-prepared — and the correct intervention is different in each case. Teachers who cannot read this distinction default to correction when co-regulation is what is actually required. Consistency Across Classrooms What delivery governance actually looks like in practice. Teacher quality at scale is not a hiring question. It is a governance question. WorldWise Learning provides the institutional architecture that moves methodology from inside individual teachers to inside the programme framework — so that delivery quality can be observed, measured, and maintained regardless of staffing. Shared Practice Standard Every WorldWise Learning teacher operates against the same observable practice standard — derived from the Thinking Cycle stages and expressed in concrete facilitation behaviours. An academic director can observe any classroom and assess delivery against the same framework, not against a personal impression of what good teaching looks like. Moderation and Calibration Teacher preparation includes moderation protocols — structured processes for calibrating what constitutes a valid Analyze response, an acceptable Justify paragraph, a genuine Reflect statement. Without moderation, standards drift silently between classrooms. Moderation is how shared standards remain shared. Staff Turnover Resilience When the methodology is inside the teacher, it leaves when the teacher leaves. When the methodology is inside the programme framework — documented, observable, and governed — a new teacher can be prepared to the same delivery standard in a defined preparation period. The programme does not restart. The methodology does not reset. Audit-Ready Practice Documentation Observable practice standards mean that teacher quality can be documented, not just described. Academic directors can produce evidence-based teacher development reports against defined criteria — not impressionistic classroom observations. This is what accreditation bodies and regulatory reviewers increasingly expect from partner programmes. For Institutional Leaders Teacher standards serve different governance needs depending on your role. The WorldWise Learning teacher preparation and delivery governance framework is designed to solve real institutional problems — not to produce compliant teachers. The people responsible for programme quality need different things from a teacher standards architecture. SME Centre Owners Delivery quality that does not depend on retaining specific teachers. If your centre's reputation depends on two or three specific teachers, you have a risk architecture problem. The WorldWise Learning framework gives you a documented delivery standard and a preparation pathway that can bring new teachers to the same quality level — so your programme quality does not walk out the door with staff. Shared delivery framework that survives staff changes New teacher preparation to defined standard — not ad hoc onboarding Observable quality indicators for all classrooms, not just your best Programme quality documented for client and parent enquiries School Leaders and Principals Teacher practice documentation that holds up to accreditation and regulatory review. MOET 2030 and international accreditation programmes increasingly require documented evidence of teacher quality — not just qualifications held, but observable practice standards applied. WorldWise Learning partnership provides the framework to produce that documentation, alongside the iPGCE baseline qualification pathway for teachers who need it. iPGCE baseline qualification pathway for all teaching staff Observable practice standards aligned to MOET 2030 teacher benchmarks Teacher development reports formatted for committee and regulatory review Accreditation-ready documentation of delivery governance Academic Directors A shared standard that can be observed, calibrated, and improved. Academic governance depends on having something to govern. Without a shared observable practice standard, academic directors are managing impressions — not practice. WorldWise Learning gives academic directors a common framework against which all teachers can be observed, all observations can be compared, and all development plans can be anchored. Common observation framework for all classrooms across the programme Moderation protocols for student work assessment calibration Structured teacher development pathway against named benchmarks Academic committee-formatted progress and compliance reporting The Next Step If teacher quality is a structural problem, the solution is structural. A Discovery Call is the most direct route to understanding how WorldWise Learning's teacher preparation and delivery governance framework would work in your specific institutional context — your team size, your current qualification baseline, and your timeline. The Discovery Call is how we scope the right entry point for your institution. ควรคำนึงถึงเงื่อนไข Writing ของเส้นทาง fast-track ไว้เสมอ แม้ในช่วงที่กำลังฝึก Speaking ผู้สมัคร Chulalongkorn ISE ควรตรวจสอบเกณฑ์ของปีการศึกษาปัจจุบันก่อนอ้างอิงข้อมูลจากรอบรับสมัครที่ผ่านมา ผู้สมัคร NTU ที่ใช้วุฒิการศึกษาของไทยควรอ่านหน้าวุฒิการศึกษาที่เกี่ยวข้องควบคู่กับเกณฑ์รายทักษะ ขณะเดียวกัน IDP Thailand ระบุว่าการสอบจัดบนคอมพิวเตอร์ ฝึกตอบออกเสียงจากคำถามที่ไม่คุ้นเคย การพูดหน้าจอในบทเรียนออนไลน์เป็นการเตรียมตัวเพื่อสื่อสารให้ชัดเจน ไม่ใช่สิ่งทดแทนการสอบ IELTS อย่างเป็นทางการ ข้อกำหนดที่มหาวิทยาลัยและหลักสูตรเผยแพร่ไว้ ข้อมูลต่อไปนี้เป็นตัวอย่างจากหน้าแหล่งข้อมูลที่ลิงก์ไว้ ไม่ใช่ผลการพิจารณารับเข้า ข้อกำหนดอาจแตกต่างกันตามรอบรับสมัคร วุฒิการศึกษา และเส้นทางการสมัคร โปรดตรวจสอบหน้าปัจจุบันของสถาบันที่จะรับผลคะแนนก่อนจองสอบอย่างเป็นทางการ เลื่อนเพื่อดูเพิ่มเติม → มหาวิทยาลัยและหลักสูตร ข้อกำหนด IELTS ที่เผยแพร่ไว้ Mahidol University International College (MUIC) — band ที่คุณต้องได้ ให้ใช้การพูดที่บันทึกเสียงไว้เพื่อหาจุดที่คุณควรพัฒนาเป็นอันดับแรกแทน ในข้อมูลของ IELTS ค่าเฉลี่ย Speaking ของผู้สอบ Academic ในไทยต่ำกว่าค่าเฉลี่ยคะแนนรวม แต่รูปแบบของกลุ่มนี้ไม่ได้บอกว่าผู้สมัคร MUIC หรือ Chulalongkorn แต่ละคนทำได้อย่างไรเมื่ออยู่ภายใต้แรงกดดัน ลองฟังว่าผู้เรียนเชื่อมจากข้อกล่าวอ้างไปสู่เหตุผล แล้วไปสู่ตัวอย่างอย่างไร คำตอบหนึ่งอาจมีคำศัพท์ที่ดี แต่ยังเชื่อมแต่ละส่วนเข้าด้วยกันไม่ได้ ครูสามารถเลือกการเชื่อมโยงนั้นเป็นจุดที่ต้องพัฒนาก่อน คำตอบครั้งต่อไปในหัวข้ออื่นจะแสดงให้เห็นว่าผู้เรียนนำสิ่งที่ปรับไปใช้ได้ด้วยตนเองหรือไม่ หน้าข้อมูลการรับสมัครต่างหาก ไม่ใช่ค่าเฉลี่ยของกลุ่ม ที่เป็นตัวกำหนดเป้าหมายอย่างเป็นทางการ การโค้ชออนไลน์สำหรับผู้เรียนในประเทศไทยทำงานอย่างไร เปิดหน้า MUIC fast-track, Chulalongkorn ISE หรือ NTU ที่ใช้กับการสมัครของคุณ การพูดครั้งแรกช่วยให้ครูวินิจฉัยปัญหาหนึ่งข้อในวิธีที่คุณเชื่อมโยงความคิด ตกลงร่วมกันว่าจะพัฒนาจุดนั้นก่อน แล้วเรียนรู้โครงสร้างที่ใช้รับมือกับคำถามที่ไม่คุ้นเคยได้ ฝึกโดยมีครูถามต่อยอด จากนั้นตอบใหม่อีกครั้งโดยไม่มีตัวช่วย แล้ววัดผลอีกครั้งว่าการเชื่อมจากความคิดเห็นไปสู่เหตุผลฟังเข้าใจง่ายขึ้นหรือไม่ สำหรับ MUIC ให้ตรวจสอบเงื่อนไข Writing ด้วย สำหรับการสมัครเรียนต่างประเทศ ให้ทบทวนเส้นทางวุฒิการศึกษาที่เกี่ยวข้อง ทั้งบทเรียนและค่าเฉลี่ยของกลุ่มไม่สามารถใช้แทนเกณฑ์การรับเข้าเหล่านั้นได้ หากต้องการตรวจระดับแบบสดเป็นครั้งแรก ดูรายละเอียด Live Speaking Baseline (มีค่าใช้จ่าย) หากต้องการเรียนกับครูอย่างต่อเนื่อง ดู ตัวเลือกการโค้ชแบบตัวต่อตัว ผู้ใหญ่อายุ 18 ปีขึ้นไป สามารถใช้ การฝึก AI Speaking ระหว่างบทเรียนได้ด้วย คำติชมจาก AI อาจผิดพลาดได้ โปรดตรวจสอบคำแนะนำที่สำคัญกับคำติชมจากมนุษย์และเกณฑ์การประเมินอย่างเป็นทางการที่เผยแพร่ต่อสาธารณะ คำถามจากผู้เรียนในประเทศไทย เส้นทาง fast-track ของ MUIC ประเมิน Writing ด้วยหรือไม่ ใช่ เส้นทางที่เผยแพร่ไว้มีเงื่อนไขด้าน Writing ควบคู่กับคะแนนรวม IDP Thailand ระบุรูปแบบการสอบแบบใด หน้าวันสอบของ IDP Thailand ที่ค้นคว้าไว้ระบุว่าการสอบ IELTS จัดบนคอมพิวเตอร์ Chulalongkorn ISE ใช้ข้อกำหนดเดียวกับ MUIC หรือไม่ ไม่ใช่ โปรดอ่านเกณฑ์การรับสมัครปัจจุบันของแต่ละสถาบันแยกกัน ฉันฝึกจากประเทศไทยได้หรือไม่ ในเมื่อการจองแสดงเวลาฮานอย ได้ โปรดแปลงเวลาเวียดนามที่แสดงก่อนยืนยันบทเรียน ก่อนจอง ยืนยันวันสอบบนคอมพิวเตอร์ของ IDP Thailand และอ่านหน้าการรับสมัครของมหาวิทยาลัยสำหรับรอบที่ถูกต้องอีกครั้ง ประเทศไทยใช้เวลาเดียวกับฮานอย แต่ยังควรตรวจสอบช่วงเวลาที่แสดงในการจอง เตรียมการพูดที่บันทึกไว้ล่าสุดมาด้วย และตรวจสอบไมโครโฟนก่อนเริ่มบทเรียน หากหลักสูตรของคุณมีเงื่อนไขด้าน Writing ด้วย ให้วางแผนเตรียมตัวสำหรับทักษะนั้นแยกต่างหาก ผลประเมินใด ๆ ระหว่างการฝึกไม่ใช่คะแนน
